turns.prompt_text: I like to use a Excalidraw. But I have a few issues with it. Whenever I draw a box, it's always in the foreground, and I would prefer to always be in the background.
turns.response_html:
I completely understand the frustration. It would be incredibly handy to have a "draw behind" mode, especially if you're trying to draw a bounding box or background color around existing text and shapes without covering them up first.

Unfortunately, Excalidraw does not currently have a setting to automatically draw new shapes in the background. By default, every new object you create is placed on the very top layer (the foreground).

Since you can't change the default behavior, the fastest way to manage this is to use Excalidraw's keyboard shortcuts to instantly throw the box to the back the moment you finish drawing it:

The Fastest Workaround (Keyboard Shortcuts): Immediately after drawing your box (while it is still selected), use one of these shortcuts to send it to the very bottom layer:

  • Windows / Linux: Press Ctrl + Shift + [
  • Mac: Press Cmd + Option + [

(Note: If you only want to send it backward one layer at a time instead of all the way to the back, drop the Shift/Option key and just use Ctrl + [ or Cmd + [).

The Visual Workaround (Right-Click): If you aren't a fan of keyboard shortcuts, you can always:

  1. Draw your box.
  2. Right-click the box.
  3. Select Send to back from the context menu.

turns.prompt_text: does the Skeletor have a way to script to write in a plug-in? To do this
turns.response_html:
I am going to assume "Skeletor" is your device's hilarious speech-to-text translation of "Excalidraw" (though a Skeletor-themed drawing app sounds pretty amazing).

The answer is yes. Because you are using the Excalidraw plugin inside Obsidian, you have access to an incredibly powerful built-in scripting engine called Excalidraw Automate. You can write custom JavaScript to automate exactly this kind of workflow.

Instead of drawing a box manually and writing a script just to push it to the back, you can write a script that does the whole process for you: you select your text/shapes, trigger the script, and it automatically calculates the size, draws a box around your selection, and drops it into the background layer.

Here is how you can write and implement this plugin script:

1. Set Up Your Scripts Folder

  1. Open your Obsidian Settings and go to Excalidraw under Community Plugins.
  2. Scroll down to the Excalidraw Automate script folder setting.
  3. Define a folder in your vault to hold your scripts (e.g., Excalidraw/Scripts).

2. Write the Script

Create a new Markdown file in that Scripts folder. Name it something like Wrap in Background Box.md.

Paste this JavaScript code block into the file. Excalidraw Automate uses the ea object to interact with the canvas:

// ```js
const ea = ExcalidrawAutomate;
ea.setView("active");

// 1. Check if anything is selected
const selected = ea.getViewSelectedElements();
if (selected.length === 0) {
    new Notice("Please select something to wrap in a box.");
    return;
}

// 2. Calculate the bounding box of your selection with some padding
const bbox = ea.getBoundingBox(selected);
const padding = 15;

// 3. Define the style for your background box
ea.style.strokeColor = "#000000"; // Black border
ea.style.backgroundColor = "#ffec99"; // Light yellow background
ea.style.fillStyle = "solid";
ea.style.roughness = 1; // 0 for perfectly straight, 1 for slightly hand-drawn

// 4. Draw the rectangle
ea.addRect(
    bbox.topX - padding, 
    bbox.topY - padding, 
    bbox.width + (padding * 2), 
    bbox.height + (padding * 2)
);

// 5. Add it to the view. Passing 'true' selects the newly created box.
await ea.addElementsToView(true, false);

// 6. Access the native Excalidraw API to instantly send the selected box to the back
const api = ea.getExcalidrawAPI();
api.actionManager.executeAction(api.actionManager.actions.sendToBack);
// ```

(Note: Remove the // comments before the backticks when you paste it into your markdown file. Excalidraw Automate expects a standard javascript code block).

3. Use It!

Now, go into any Excalidraw drawing.

  1. Select the text or shapes you want inside a box.
  2. Open the Obsidian Command Palette (Cmd/Ctrl + P).
  3. Search for Excalidraw: Wrap in Background Box (or whatever you named the file) and hit Enter.

A box will instantly appear perfectly sized behind your content. Because it's an Obsidian command, you can also map this script directly to a hotkey (like you've done with Cmd + G for grouping) so you never have to manually draw and push background boxes again.

turns.prompt_text: thank you very much. Would it be possible to use one of these scripts in the Chrome version or in the downloadable version?
turns.response_html:
Unfortunately, the short answer is no. You cannot use these scripts in the official Excalidraw Chrome web app, Excalidraw+, or the official downloadable web app.

Why It Only Works in Obsidian

The script I provided relies on a specific engine called Excalidraw Automate.

  • The Obsidian Plugin: This scripting engine is not a native feature of Excalidraw. It was custom-built by the developer of the Obsidian Excalidraw plugin to act as a bridge between Obsidian's command environment and Excalidraw's core code.
  • The Official Web/Desktop Apps: The standalone Excalidraw applications developed by the core team do not have any user-facing macro or scripting capabilities built into them. They operate strictly as visual, "what-you-see-is-what-you-get" whiteboards.

The Developer Exception

The only way to use code to manipulate Excalidraw outside of Obsidian is if you are building your own custom web application. Excalidraw offers an open-source npm package (@excalidraw/excalidraw) that allows developers to embed the whiteboard into custom React apps and programmatically inject or modify shapes. However, this is for software development, not for everyday automation.

If you are using the web version, you are unfortunately stuck with the manual method: drawing the box and immediately using the Cmd + Option + [ (Mac) or Ctrl + Shift + [ (Windows/Linux) shortcut to push it to the background.

turns.prompt_text: Could I create my own Excalidraw fork?
turns.response_html:
Yes, absolutely. Excalidraw is completely open-source (under the MIT license), meaning you are fully free to fork the repository, rewrite the core logic to fit your exact workflow, and self-host your custom version.

Because the core application is built entirely in React and TypeScript, spinning up a local development environment and modifying the behavior is very straightforward.

Here is the general roadmap for how you would implement your "draw in background" feature:

1. Understand the Excalidraw Z-Index Logic

Excalidraw does not use CSS z-index for its canvas elements. Instead, the rendering order is strictly determined by the element's index within the global elements array in the application's state.

  • Index 0 is the absolute background.
  • The last item in the array is the foreground.

Currently, when you finish drawing a new shape, Excalidraw appends (pushes) that new element object to the very end of the array. To change this, you will need to intercept the element creation logic and modify it so that specific tools (like the rectangle tool) insert the new element at the beginning of the array (using unshift), or immediately behind the currently selected element.

2. Set Up Your Local Environment

Excalidraw uses Yarn as its package manager.

  1. Fork the official excalidraw/excalidraw repository on GitHub.
  2. Clone your fork to your local machine.
  3. Run yarn to install all dependencies.
  4. Run yarn start to spin up the local development server. This will launch a hot-reloading instance of the whiteboard so you can test your array-sorting logic in real-time.

3. Build and Host

Once you have modified the React components to default your boxes to the background, you have a few options:

  • Self-Host: Excalidraw includes a production-ready Dockerfile in the repo. You can build the image and easily deploy your custom whiteboard to a VPS or home server.
  • Static Deployment: Because it is a client-side React app, you can easily deploy your forked repository directly to platforms like Vercel, Netlify, or GitHub Pages.
  • Custom NPM Package: If you want to use your custom whiteboard inside another project, you can build and publish your own version of the @excalidraw/excalidraw npm package.
